Mexico

Two Coasts,
Two Different Trips.

Riviera Maya and Los Cabos get sold as the same holiday and they could hardly be less alike. One is jungle, cenotes and Caribbean water with Mayan ruins an hour inland. The other is desert meeting Pacific, with a sea that is often too rough to swim and a restaurant scene that has quietly become the best in the country. Choosing correctly between them is most of the work.

The Two Coasts

The same country, two entirely different weeks.

November through April is the window for both coasts. Most trips run 5–9 days. The Riviera Maya has warm swimmable Caribbean water, cenotes and Mayan sites; Los Cabos has desert landscape, golf, whales and the better restaurant scene. Sargassum can be significant on parts of the Riviera Maya between roughly April and October, and absent a few miles away.

The Riviera Maya runs south from Cancún along the Caribbean: flat, hot, jungle-backed, with water that genuinely is the colour of the brochures. It is also the most overbuilt coastline in Mexico, which means the gap between an excellent property and a disappointing one is enormous and almost invisible from a booking site. Tulum in particular has changed beyond recognition in five years, and not always for the better.

Los Cabos sits at the tip of Baja, where the desert falls into the Pacific. The landscape is dramatic rather than pretty, the water is frequently not swimmable, and the appeal is elsewhere: the golf, the whale season, the sportfishing, and a dining scene that now justifies the trip on its own. It suits travellers who want a resort week with texture, and disappoints anyone expecting Caribbean calm.

Where to Go

The Areas That Actually Differ

Mexico rewards choosing the right stretch of coast far more than choosing the right hotel brand.

Riviera Maya
Playa del Carmen to Tulum
The Caribbean coast proper. Cenotes for swimming, Mayan sites at Cobá and Chichén Itzá in the mornings, and beachfront properties of wildly varying quality. We know which avoid seaweed season.
Plan This Trip →
Baja California Sur
Los Cabos & the Corridor
San José del Cabo at one end, Cabo San Lucas at the other, and a twenty-mile corridor between them. The corridor is where the serious properties sit. Choose by beach: many are not swimmable.
Plan This Trip →
The Quiet Alternative
Todos Santos & the East Cape
An hour from the Cabo airport and a different country in feel. Small hotels, surf beaches, no cruise traffic. For travellers who want Baja without the resort corridor, this is the answer of choice.
Plan This Trip →
Inland
Yucatán & Mérida
Two hours from the coast and almost never included, which is a shame. Colonial Mérida, restored haciendas, and the Mayan sites without the day-trip crowds. The strongest addition to a week.

The Details

What We Add to Mexico Planning

This is the coastline where good planning saves a holiday most often, because the failure modes are invisible in advance.

⬡
The Seaweed Question
Sargassum season runs roughly April to October and affects the Riviera Maya coast unevenly — some beaches badly, others barely. It is the single most common reason a Mexico trip disappoints, and it is entirely avoidable with the right timing and the right stretch of sand.
⬡
Swimmable or Not
Large parts of the Los Cabos coastline have dangerous surf and no safe swimming. Resorts do not advertise this. We book by beach first and property second, which is the reverse of how most Cabo trips are planned.
⬡
Property Reality
The Riviera Maya has more new-build luxury than anywhere in the Americas and the quality range is severe. We have stayed in them. The recommendation is based on the current state of the property, not the brochure or the year it opened.
⬡
Beyond the Resort
Private cenote access before the tour buses, archaeologists rather than guides at the Mayan sites, and the restaurants that locals book. The difference between a Mexico week and a Mexico week worth remembering.
When to Go

Mexico by Season

The two coasts run on different calendars, which is useful — there is almost always one of them at its best.

The Sweet Spot
November – April
Dry, warm, and clear on both coasts. Minimal sargassum risk on the Caribbean side, whale season in Baja from January. The obvious window, priced accordingly.
Best Window
Shoulder
May & October
Warmer and quieter, with real value at properties that are otherwise difficult. Sargassum becomes a factor on the Riviera Maya — worth taking advice on the specific beach before booking.
Summer
June – September
Hot, humid and wet on the Caribbean coast, with hurricane season overlapping. Los Cabos holds up better. For flexible travellers the pricing is genuinely compelling.

What It Costs

What Mexico's coasts Actually Cost

$450–$1,200
per person, per night. Ranges, not quotes.
What that includes
  • Half of a five-star or boutique room, breakfast where the property bundles it
  • The 16% IVA and the state lodging tax on the room rate
  • Beach and pool service, Wi-Fi and gym access
What it does not
  • International airfare, airport transfers and each state's per-person visitor tax
  • Lunch, dinner and alcohol unless the property is all-inclusive
  • Excursions, cenote and Mayan-site entry, spa, golf and gratuities
The two or three things that move it most
  • Room category — a beachfront suite tops the band, a garden room sits near the floor
  • Meal plan — an all-inclusive rate absorbs those meals and prices above room-only
  • Dates — peak nights at the Cabo flagships run over twice their off-peak rate

Editorial planning bands, not quotes — assembled from published rates and official fee sources, verified August 2026. Rates, permit costs and park fees change; confirm before booking. Source: Mexico's IVA rate (Ley del IVA, Article 1).

Common Questions

Riviera Maya & Los Cabos — FAQ

Questions we hear most when planning Riviera Maya & Los Cabos trips. More detail on the full FAQ page.

Riviera Maya for warm swimmable Caribbean water, cenotes and Mayan culture. Los Cabos for dramatic desert landscape, golf, whales and the better restaurant scene. If swimming from the beach is central to the trip, the Riviera Maya wins most of the time.

It varies enormously by beach and by year. Between roughly April and October it can be significant on parts of the Riviera Maya and almost absent a few miles away. It is a planning problem rather than a reason to avoid Mexico, but it does need planning.

Some are outstanding and some are a way of guaranteeing you never leave the property. On this coast we usually recommend the all-inclusive for families and a room-only or half-board property for couples, because the restaurants outside the resort are half the reason to come.

The tourist corridors of Quintana Roo and Baja California Sur are heavily policed and see very few problems. Standard precautions apply as in any resort destination. We advise on specific areas and on ground transport, which is the part most people get wrong.

It is a five-hour flight between them, so it only makes sense on a longer trip. More often we pair one coast with something inland — Mérida and the haciendas from the Riviera Maya, or Todos Santos and the East Cape from Los Cabos.

For Christmas, New Year and Easter, six to nine months. The best rooms at the strongest properties go early and do not come back. Outside those windows, three months is usually comfortable.
